meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It's déjà vu all over again'?
meta.ogDescription: Berra denied it, then claimed it. The line was in print by 1966 — and no one linked it to him until 1984.

answer.label: Not Yogi Berra — earliest known in print
answer.authorDates: Chicago Tribune film critic · earliest documented use, 22 February 1966
answer.sourceLine: The earliest appearance Quote Investigator has found for the full wording is Clifford Terry’s Chicago Tribune review of the Dean Martin spy comedy “The Silencers,” 22 February 1966; a 1962 newspaper poem by Jim Prior had already used the shorter “It’s Deja Vu again.” Nothing links the line to Yogi Berra until 1984 — and Berra flatly denied saying it in 1987 and again in his 1989 autobiography before claiming it in 1998. Quote Investigator stops short of naming a coiner, and so does this page: what is documented is who printed it first, not who invented it.

source.excerpt: It’s déjà vu all over again—the usual gaggle of gimmicks …
trail: 1962 — the closest early relative is a love poem, “Thanks To You” by Jim Prior, printed in the Evening Independent on 22 September 1962: “It’s Deja Vu again / Out of the blue again.” Quote Investigator ↗
1966 — the full comic wording appears in print: Chicago Tribune critic Clifford Terry, 22 February 1966, p. B5, on “The Silencers.” No mention of Yogi Berra. Quote Investigator ↗

1984 — the first known printing that connects the line to Berra: a Wall Street Journal story of 20 July 1984 carrying “As Yogi Berra would say, this is deja vu all over again.” Wikiquote gives the same 1984 threshold. Wikiquote ↗
1987, 1989, then 1998 — Berra denied it to William Safire and again in Yogi: It Ain’t Over (McGraw-Hill, 1989), then claimed it in The Yogi Book (Workman, 1998). Internet Archive ↗
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator from the Chicago Tribune of 22 February 1966; the piece is a review of the Dean Martin spy comedy “The Silencers.” This is the earliest printing of the full wording that has been located — not proof of who coined it. Quote Investigator ↗

source.rightsNote: Authorship of the phrase is unresolved, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for the line itself. Nothing in the paper trail is public domain either: the earliest documented printings — the 1962 newspaper poem and the Chicago Tribune of 22 February 1966 — both fall well after the 1931 US public-domain threshold, as do Berra’s own books of 1989, 1998 and 2003.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.heading: The man it’s pinned on
author.metaLine: 1925–2015 · Yankees catcher, manager and accidental aphorist
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra caught for the New York Yankees from 1946 to 1963, won ten World Series titles as a player — more than anyone in major-league history — made 18 All-Star teams, took three American League MVP awards, and later managed both the Yankees and the Mets. He became at least as famous for his looping, self-cancelling one-liners, and was unusually candid about how many of them were not his: he titled his 1998 collection The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!

misattribution.heading: The credit, the denial, the reversal
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-quoted “Yogi-isms” on earth. It is also the one Berra himself spent more than a decade insisting was not his.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line under Disputed, noting that it is found in a poem by Jim Prior published in a Florida newspaper in 1962, that Berra claimed to have made the remark around 1961, and that the earliest published evidence linking the saying to him does not appear until 1984. Wikiquote ↗

Telephoned by New York Times language columnist William Safire in 1987, Berra answered “Nope, not true, I never said that,” and repeated it in print in his 1989 autobiography Yogi: It Ain’t Over: “I didn’t say, ‘It’s déjà vu all over again.’” Quote Investigator ↗

In The Yogi Book (Workman, 1998) he embraced the line and gave it a setting — watching Mickey Mantle and Roger Maris hit back-to-back home runs, around 1961. No contemporary record of that remark has been produced. Professor Buzzkill ↗

Reference works and tribute round-ups still print it as a plain Berra quotation. CBS Sports, sorting the genuine Yogi-isms from the borrowed ones, noted that Berra “told the Times language columnist William Safire in 1987 that he never said it, but later in life was known to take credit for it.” CBS Sports ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The safest true sentence: no source has ever been produced for Yogi Berra saying it, the wording was already running in American newspapers by 1966, and the first person on record attaching it to Berra was a Wall Street Journal writer in July 1984. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it stuck to him anyway
lead: By the mid-1980s Yogi Berra had stopped being only a person and become a category of joke. Once a line had the right looping, self-cancelling shape, editors reached for his name to introduce it — and the first known printing that puts this line next to Berra, a Wall Street Journal story of 20 July 1984, does exactly that, safely hedged as “As Yogi Berra would say.” The hedge did not survive long: by 1985 papers were printing it as something Berra had simply said. Quote Investigator ↗

The strangest turn is Berra’s own. He said no for years, then said yes, and supplied a scene to go with it: Mickey Mantle and Roger Maris hitting back-to-back home runs, around 1961. No contemporary record of that remark has ever surfaced. Memory is a poor witness at that distance, particularly after a decade of being told by everyone around you that you said it. Professor Buzzkill ↗
context.detailsSummary: The citation ladder, rung by rung
detailsBody: Between the 1966 Tribune review and the first Berra attribution, the joke circulated with no owner at all. Quote Investigator records it in Chicago Metro News in 1979 (“If we have another snow storm, it’ll be deja vu all over again”) and in the Washington Post in 1981, where Tish Baldrige used it about a White House redecoration. Quote Investigator ↗

The first printing that names Berra is the Wall Street Journal of 20 July 1984: “As Yogi Berra would say, this is deja vu all over again.” Within a year the qualifier was gone — the Dallas Morning News in 1985 had “Like Yogi Berra once said, it was deja vu all over again.” Quote Investigator ↗
context.pull: “Nope, not true, I never said that.” — Berra to William Safire, 1987
